title: How does CSRF protection work in ASP.NET Core?
description: Why cookie-based auth needs antiforgery tokens, how SameSite helps, and when bearer tokens change the story.

data.text: **Question:** How does CSRF protection work in ASP.NET Core?

CSRF (cross-site request forgery) tricks an already-authenticated victim's browser into submitting a forged request — the browser attaches the session cookie automatically, so the server can't tell the request from a legitimate one. ASP.NET Core issues a **per-session antiforgery token** that the client must echo back (hidden form field or `X-CSRF-TOKEN` header); attackers on another origin can't read it, so the forged request fails validation. SameSite cookies are a strong second layer, not a replacement.

**How the attack works:**
- You are logged into `bank.example` — its session cookie is stored
- You visit `evil.example`, which silently auto-submits a form POST to `bank.example/transfer`
- Your browser attaches the bank cookie (same-site request from its point of view)
- Without extra checks, the transfer executes as you

**Why the token defeats it:**
- The token is generated server-side, bound to your session, and stored where cross-origin scripts cannot read it (form field / HttpOnly-protected flow, or a readable non-HttpOnly cookie echoed in a header — the double-submit pattern)
- The attacker can cause a request, but cannot **read** the token to include it, so validation fails and the request is rejected (400)

**SameSite as layer two:**
- `Lax` (modern browser default) withholds cookies on cross-site POSTs and most subrequests, while still sending them on top-level GET navigations
- `Strict` withholds everything cross-site, but breaks links into your site from external emails
- `None` must be paired with `Secure` and re-enables cross-site cookie sending — rarely right for session cookies

**When CSRF does not apply:**
- Pure bearer-token APIs (token in the `Authorization` header) — browsers never attach those automatically
- The trap: accepting **both** cookie auth and bearer auth for the same unsafe endpoints re-opens CSRF for the cookie path

data.text:
Interviewers want to assess:
- Understanding that CSRF rides on **cookie credentials**, not on a code bug
- Knowledge of the token flow in both server-rendered forms and SPAs
- That SameSite helps but is a complement, not the whole answer
- The distinction between CSRF (cookie) and XSS (script execution)

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: CSRF exploits automatically-attached cookies on cross-site requests
Antiforgery tokens must be echoed back — attackers can't read them cross-origin
SameSite=Lax/Strict is a strong second layer; None requires Secure
Bearer-header APIs aren't CSRF-vulnerable unless they also accept cookies
data.takeaway: For cookie-authenticated apps: validate an unguessable per-session token on every unsafe request, keep SameSite strict-ish, and never mutate state on GET.
